name: The St. Regis Kuala Lumpur
description:
The St. Regis Kuala Lumpur sits in KL Sentral, the city’s main transport interchange. It opened in 2016 with 208 rooms and suites, and its function space runs across four floors.

The Grand Ballroom is the largest of its rooms, at roughly 1,300 square metres, and seats 990 for a banquet or 850 standing. A 270-degree LED canvas of 47 screens wraps three sides of it, and a private lift big enough to hold a car opens directly into the room.

The Astor Room is the junior ballroom. It has a separate entrance for private drop-offs and its own pre-event space for cocktails. The Salon is kept for weddings and VIP events, with a lounge, a dressing room, and a live video feed from the Grand Ballroom. Crystal, the rooftop bar, runs over two levels with a pool and an LED media wall, and can be booked for events.

Smaller rooms include the State Room, the Drawing Room, the Exchange Lounge, the Dollar and Ringgit rooms, a screening room, and the Decanter wine room.

description:
Jazz Hotel Penang is a 4-star waterfront hotel in Seri Tanjung Pinang, Tanjung Tokong, a short walk from Straits Quay. It takes its theme from the Jazz Age, and the interiors follow through: a neon saxophonist mural over the lobby seating, brass gramophones, a grand piano against red velvet curtains. There are 255 guestrooms, every one with a bathtub, and a rooftop infinity pool on Level 30 that looks out over the strait.

The event spaces are on Levels 8 and 9, and they are genuinely small. The hotel describes four event halls of varying sizes, two of which combine into one larger room, and puts the ceiling at roughly 130 guests. At ten to a table that is about thirteen tables. This is a venue for a solemnisation, a tea ceremony, or an intimate dinner rather than a full banquet, and couples planning for 300 should look elsewhere. All four halls have built-in LED screens. Outdoors, the hotel markets its courtyard for intimate weddings and receptions, though it publishes no photographs or dimensions for it.

The hotel has not published capacities for the individual halls, wedding packages, or banquet menus, so those are worth asking about directly. We have not yet featured a wedding here, and the hotel's own marketing is the only evidence of its wedding work that we found.

description:
Four Hands sits behind a wall of glass on Jalan Burma, a few minutes from the George Town heritage core. It opened in November 2024 and spends its daytime as a dim sum restaurant, serving breakfast and lunch until 6pm.

The room couples come for is the Glass House — a freestanding steel-and-glass pavilion in the courtyard, built under a mature tree against the exposed brick of a neighbouring party wall. Its pitched glass roof lets the light and the branches in, and sheer white drapes run the length of both glazed walls. The venue sets it two ways: theatre-style with an aisle down the middle for the ceremony, or with long banquet tables and round tables for the dinner. A 2m by 4m LED screen sits at the head of the room, with a basic PA system and two microphones.

Indoors, the Heritage dining hall is the larger space: white marble floors, columns, a bar along one side and a staircase at the back, laid with a mix of long tables and rounds. Five private rooms sit off it, each enclosed, air-conditioned and fitted with its own screen and karaoke console — the largest takes a round table of about fourteen, the smallest a table of eight.

The venue publishes two priced documents. Its ROM package runs three hours of exclusive use of the Glass House from 2:30pm to 5:30pm for up to 20 guests, at RM3,888++, and includes a canapé spread, free-flow drinks, a two-tier cake, a champagne fountain with a bottle of sparkling wine, a dressed signing table and photo props. For dinner, the Eternal Menu is an eight-course Chinese banquet at RM2,388++ per table of ten, opening with a five-item deluxe platter and running through shark fin soup, roast duck, steamed grouper, salted egg prawns and braised abalone.

This is a restaurant that hosts weddings, not a hotel ballroom. Couples planning something intimate will find it a natural fit; anyone planning a large banquet should ask about numbers, since the venue publishes no overall capacity.

description:
Sentul Depot is the railway works inside Sentul Park, restored by YTL Land as part of the Sentul Masterplan. The workshops where locomotives were once assembled and repaired are now let as event space, and they have been left much as they were found: brick walls, steel trusses, saw-tooth factory roofs, and in the largest workshop the original zinc roofing brought over from England.

Four spaces are on the 2026 events rate card. The Yard is the biggest and sits centrally between the workshops, so it takes the largest weddings. Workshop 1 is a barn-like 1960s annex, fully covered, with ceilings high enough for big installations. Workshop 3 is the air-conditioned one, raw brick with tall steel-framed glass, and it is the space the depot itself points weddings toward. The Control Room is a small first-floor room for whatever runs alongside the main event.

The rate buys the space and the day. Catering, furniture, styling and any power beyond the house supply come in with your own suppliers, under the depot’s house rules. It suits couples who want to build the day from scratch rather than pick a package.
